What mature systems actually do

You asked where Tesla, Amazon, healthcare standards, and serious engineering organizations put this.

I cannot verify Tesla’s private folder structure. Anyone pretending otherwise is guessing. The public automotive analogue is AUTOSAR: it standardizes reusable application interfaces and semantics so applications can be exchanged or reused across projects and hardware, while deliberately not standardizing each application’s internal algorithm.

The broader established pattern is not one clever memo. It is a stack:

OMNI need	Established analogue	Mechanism
Shared architecture core	SEI software product lines	Products come from a reusable core asset base; variability is modeled explicitly instead of rebuilt ad hoc. SEI names duplicate mechanisms, incompatible variation choices, and missed variations as the failure modes of unmanaged variability—the exact failure occurring here.
Domain/local specialization	FHIR profiles and Implementation Guides	Base resources are restricted and extended for domains, countries, institutions, and implementations; conformance artifacts make those adaptations computable. A system may conform to multiple profiles, with compatibility rules.
Actor/interaction composition	IHE Integration Profiles	Profiles specify actors, required transactions, optionality, and required groupings. A product can implement multiple actors and profiles, but must expose every required transaction to claim conformance.
Cross-cutting review overlays	AWS Well-Architected lenses	A core framework is applied to every workload; multiple official or custom lenses add domain-specific questions, best practices, and improvement plans.
Proof and traceability	NASA systems engineering	Each normative “shall” is uniquely identified, traced to its source, and connected to a defined verification method and result.

So no: serious organizations do not rebuild braking, collision avoidance, steering, fulfillment, returns, identity, safety, and evidence from first principles inside every department.

They establish:

a reference architecture;
reusable core assets;
standardized interfaces;
explicit variability;
implementation profiles;
compliance matrices;
and executable verification.

The company-specific magic lives in which laws and modules they choose, not in pretending variation management does not exist.

What OMNI actually needs

The answer is not another single giant doctrine file.

It is a maintained architecture package.

1. OMNI Kernel — working name, not yet canon

This is the authoritative build-facing architecture core.

It contains only reusable, cross-loop material:

universal constitutional laws;
recurring architectural modules;
each module’s authority and maturity;
required owners;
forbidden collapses;
variation points;
correction behavior;
counterexamples;
required conformance tests.

Candidate modules would include—but are not limited to:

evidence → attributed meaning → adoption
intent → admissibility → commitment → consequence
request/order → acceptance → fulfillment → proof
external-principal participation
obligation/custody continuity
versioned definition/policy
source-preserving projection
governed resolution and reopening

These are not final names or a completed list.

Reactor would likely live here as the intent-to-consequence / consequential-transition module, assuming it eventually passes its remaining promotion requirements.

2. OMNI Profiles

Each concrete operating profile declares exactly how it uses the Kernel.

An Insurance profile would say, structurally:

instantiates:
  - external_principal_participation
  - governed_resolution
  - obligation_continuity
  - source_preserving_projection

inherits:
  - source authority
  - proposal != commitment
  - payment state != care state
  - correction preserves history
  - projection != authority

specializes:
  - coverage relationship
  - funding condition
  - benefit interpretation
  - determination / appeal / recoupment
  - financing arrangement
  - patient responsibility

does_not_inherit:
  - clinical adoption authority
  - pharmacist professional authority
  - universal execution veto from payer funding

native_truth_owners:
  ...

required_conformance:
  ...

open_variances:
  ...

Pharmacy would instantiate some of the same modules and specialize others.

Labs would instantiate evidence/adoption and fulfillment/counterparty modules.

One profile may use several modules. One module may serve many profiles.

That avoids both extremes:

one god-model for everything;
every lane inventing its own physics.
3. OMNI Conformance Suite

Every inherited law needs proof.

That means:

machine-readable profile declarations where practical;
fixtures;
seeded violations;
compatibility checks;
source/authority/correction tests;
portability tests;
experience tests;
and explicit unresolved variances.

C4.6’s C1–C16 and Reactor’s conformance work are seeds of this, not the entire suite.

4. The spine

The spine states, concisely:

what the Kernel is;
why it exists;
the major constitutional commitments;
and how Profiles compile it into real operating systems.

It points to the build-facing Kernel.

It does not carry every field, profile, fixture, and compatibility rule itself.

5. The control plane and Build Entry

The existing control plane then performs its proper function:

catalog;
authority;
supersession;
routing;
required read graph.

And Build Entry enforces:

no new loop/profile can open or close without declaring its Kernel inheritance, specialization, non-inheritance, owners, and conformance obligations.

That is the missing mechanism.

This is not proof OMNI is hopeless.

Decision

Yes. It is a real thing.

Insurance pauses. We open a dedicated foundational architecture reconciliation-and-installation arc now.

Not an “OMNI kernel” branding exercise.
Not another Reactor essay.
Not an index-only control-plane patch.
Not a fifth round of free-form synthesis that ends with “future agents should remember this.”

The thing you are reaching for is:

OMNI’s maintained, build-facing system for turning cross-OMNI laws and recurring interaction physics into concrete operating profiles, contracts, and conformance proofs.

That system does not currently exist in a coherent, current, authoritative, usable form.

Pieces of it exist. Some are strong. Some are stale. Some are binding only as posture. Some are review drafts. Some are closed evidence runs. Some are buried inside domain work. Some are universally routed but obsolete. None currently tells a builder, reliably and completely:

which OMNI-wide laws apply;
which reusable architecture patterns are being instantiated;
which parts are specialized for this domain or counterparty;
which pieces must not be inherited;
which owners retain truth and commit authority;
which failure behaviors must survive;
and what tests must pass before the profile can be called OMNI-conformant.

That is why Care, Pharmacy, Reactor, GCE, and Insurance have repeatedly rediscovered one another.

Where I disagree with Opus

Opus’s latest recommendation is:

do not open a foundation arc; create a small transaction containing an index, some routing, a Build Entry obligation, and a decision on the May file.

That is not enough.

An index can tell the next agent that five conflicting or differently matured ideas exist. It cannot determine:

whether those ideas are actually the same law;
whether one supersedes another;
whether one is a specialization of another;
whether Reactor is the parent, child, sibling, or unrelated composition;
whether the May three-layer pattern remains universal;
whether Care’s admissibility decomposition is constitutional or care-specific;
whether GCE is a reusable pattern, a universal edge contract, or merely doctrine-level posture;
how profiles inherit these things;
or which tests prove a profile has compiled them correctly.

A pointer-only transaction would make the mess more discoverable, not make the architecture coherent.

That is useful bookkeeping. It is not the missing architecture.

Your objection is correct: the index and rules cannot be invented on the fly and then mistaken for the thing we are trying to build. The architecture itself must be reconciled, authored, installed, and enforced.

Where I disagree with the old Reactor closeout

The Reactor terminus said not to reopen the conceptual arc absent narrow triggers and directed the next proof into the real world. The completed successor run did produce an executable fixture and independent adjudication, while leaving Reactor frozen and unpromoted.

That closeout can legitimately say:

do not endlessly re-derive Reactor’s eight invariants;
do not add a ninth invariant because a new chat sounds clever;
do not create a central reactor-service;
do not claim production proof from a conformance fixture.

It cannot legitimately mean:

“Do not reconcile Reactor against later Care, Pharmacy, GCE, the May architecture pattern, Build Entry, or Insurance, even when those artifacts contradict, duplicate, or fail to inherit one another.”

That is outside its scope.

It was an analysis_nonbinding run terminus, not a constitutional prohibition on future architecture work. And its own reopening rule allowed explicit Nick-and-Knox direction. You have now explicitly challenged the closeout’s installation failure.

More fundamentally, the old closeout conflated two different questions:

Has this architecture concept earned a durable, honest place in OMNI’s architecture?
Has this concept been proven in production, accepted by external parties, and shown to create economic or safety value?

Those are not the same maturity gate.

An architecture module can be installed as:

candidate architecture
well-defined
source-reconciled
build-facing
not production-proven
not externally accepted

We do that constantly with draft contracts and pre-build architecture.

Requiring real-world pharmacy adoption before the concept is allowed to have a usable architectural home was over-gating. It left the concept frozen in evidence artifacts while later builders continued solving the same problem without it.

The thing is not Reactor alone

This remains the other major correction.

Reactor

Reactor is the strongest current candidate for consequential-transition continuity:

admissibility before consequence;
domain-owned commitment;
accepted custody;
no silent orphaning;
selective reopening;
compensation versus remedy versus reconsideration versus outcome;
honest projection;
bounded proof.

That is substantial. It is not all of OMNI.

The missing architecture, functionally

Do not name it yet.

Use the working description:

OMNI Foundational Architecture System

That is a lane label, not the final brand.

It has four required parts.

1. OMNI-wide constitutional laws

The genuinely universal imperatives:

authoritative state remains owned;
candidate is not commit;
consent and authority remain distinct;
payment state does not author care state;
projection does not become authority;
historical consequence is not erased by compensation;
cross-boundary exchange preserves principal, authority, context, consent, commit, and proof;
unresolved consequence cannot silently disappear;
and whatever else survives the full reconciliation.

This is where Polaris, Tier‑0 laws, parts of Reactor, GCE, and the cross-cutting Care laws meet.

2. Reusable architecture patterns

Not universal truth objects. Reusable compositions.

Likely candidates include:

evidence → verification → attributed meaning → adoption;
intent → admissibility → commitment → consequence;
request/order → acceptance → execution → proof;
external-principal participation;
obligation/custody continuity;
governed resolution and reopening;
source-preserving projection;
versioned definition/policy;
exchange through GCE.

The arc must determine the actual set. That list is not pre-approved.

3. Operating profiles

A profile declares how a particular area uses the shared architecture.

An Insurance profile might instantiate:

external-principal participation
governed resolution
obligation continuity
source-preserving projection
GCE exchange

and specialize:

coverage relationship
funding condition
benefit interpretation
determination
appeal
recoupment
financing arrangement
patient responsibility

while explicitly refusing to inherit:

clinical adoption authority
pharmacist professional authority
payer veto over clinical indication
universal care-blocking power from payment state

Pharmacy, Labs, Scheduling, Payroll, Gmail, and Banking would have different combinations.

4. Conformance and compilation

Every profile must identify:

inherited laws;
specialized laws;
non-inherited laws;
source-truth owners;
commit owners;
accepted variation points;
open variances;
correction behavior;
failure states;
human operating outcomes;
required tests.

Then Build Entry blocks work that cannot prove conformance.

That is what makes the architecture real.

This is a known engineering problem

We are not inventing the general mechanism.

Software product-line engineering builds portfolios from a reusable core asset base and explicitly models planned variability. The SEI specifically warns that unmanaged variability causes duplicate mechanisms, incompatible variation choices, unnecessary variation, and missed required variations—the exact pathology OMNI has demonstrated.

FHIR uses a base specification plus profiles and Implementation Guides. It explicitly anticipates overlapping adaptations by healthcare domain, country, institution, and vendor. Its conformance resources make inherited and specialized constraints computable rather than leaving them as prose.

So yes:

The thing is real in normal architecture.

OMNI’s distinctive contribution is not inventing profiles or reference architectures.

It is deciding which healthcare and care-business laws must survive every profile, especially where principals are sovereign, misaligned, external, or adversarial.

Six statements, one law, zero addresses. That is not a taxonomy debate — it's a build defect that costs an arc every time.

**Where I disagree with Knox, and it's the whole difference between this working and being pass five.** Knox wants read-everything → synthesize → pressure → install. That is the big bang, it burns a million tokens before anything is testable, and it's precisely what you predicted would happen. So the charter rejects it and takes your outpost instead — build one thing out of real materials and see if it stands.

Concretely: drive **one law** end-to-end through the entire machinery before reconciling anything. `payment state ≠ care state`, from constitutional statement → reusable pattern → four profile declarations (Insurance, Pharmacy, Gmail, payroll/bank) → conformance test → build-entry obligation → read route. I picked that law deliberately because it's the hard case, not the easy one: it's contracted on the D6 side and **owed on the Care side**, so the machinery has to be able to say *"inherited here, missing there"* — which is the thing an index can never do. And it already has runnable test seeds in `C6` and `C12`, so the conformance half isn't hypothetical.

If one law can't make that trip, the system isn't real and we found out in one slice. **Gate 1 can return `NOT_A_SYSTEM` and that closes the arc and sends us back to Insurance.** I wrote that in as a real, permitted outcome, because an arc that can only succeed is theatre.

**I concede the index point entirely.** You were right and I was wrong. Ten artifacts at ten maturities that contradict each other, listed in one place, makes the mess discoverable without making the architecture coherent. "The index with the rules is the thing we're trying to build" is the correct refutation and I don't have a counter.

**Where it lives — this one has an answer and it isn't a guess.** The Surface Map declares the plane taxonomy `P0`–`P6`. And we've already created canonical hub artifacts per plane group, twice, both at `.cursor/plans/` root: `OMNI_System_Map_vNext.md` is the hub for P1 Truth, `OMNI_Surface_Map_vNext.md` is the hub for P4/P5. **The missing hub is the cross-plane one — what every loop must obey and how it declares compliance. Its home is a peer of those two, same place, same convention.** Not `doctrine/` (that's ledgers and process). Not `contracts/` (that's per-domain truth). **On "the document must just BE the document" — that's a solved problem and it has a name: the normative/informative split.** RFC 2119 separates `MUST/SHOULD/MAY` normative text from discussion. FHIR separates the machine-readable StructureDefinition from the Implementation Guide narrative. AWS separates the framework questions from the whitepapers. So the output shape is: **one terse numbered normative artifact a builder reads alone, with a machine-checkable half wherever possible, and all the rationale and lineage in separate informative carriers.** We already have two working examples of the machine-checkable half in this repo — the checkpoint-pointer checker and the 31/31 consequential-transition fixture. Decision

Yes. What you are describing is a real, necessary part of OMNI.

And the current Gate‑0 charter is not accepted as written, because Opus misunderstood the outpost and inserted an unnecessary existential test.

There will be:

no additional payment state ≠ care state pilot;
no Gate‑1 test to determine whether the architecture system exists;
no possibility that the arc returns NOT_A_SYSTEM;
no return to Insurance until this foundational architecture is installed.

The recurrence across Care, GCE, Pharmacy, Reactor, Platform, Accountability, the May architecture pattern, and Insurance has already answered the existence question. The remaining questions are its exact structure, content, authority, name, and installation.

The straight answers
Question	Answer
Is this a thing?	Yes. Decided.
Is the whole thing OMNI Reactor?	No. Reactor is one major module inside it.
Is it merely a third sibling beside the System Map and Surface Map?	No. It is the parent architecture system in which those maps, Reactor, GCE, profiles, contracts, and conformance have typed places.
Is it a white paper?	No. Its controlling core is a normative architecture specification.
Does it get a separate explanatory document?	Yes. Thesis/spine/rationale explain it; they do not substitute for it.
Does it finally live in .cursor/plans/?	No. That may hold the temporary arc materials, but not the final architecture.
Do we pay the large reconciliation cost now?	Yes—once, deliberately, against controlling termini.
Does Insurance stay frozen?	Yes.

I reviewed the supplied Opus reasoning, its correction trail, the R1 relay, and the aviation extraction as part of this decision.

What the thing actually is

The clearest functional description is:

OMNI’s canonical, cross-plane architecture constitution and profile system: the build-facing source that states OMNI-wide laws, defines reusable architectural patterns, declares how concrete operating profiles specialize them, and specifies the conformance proof required before anything is built.

That description is intentionally functional. The proper name can come from you after the architecture has acquired a recognizable form.

This is not one more domain, lifecycle, god-object, control plane, or ontology.

It is the architecture system over those things.

Its four parts
1. Architecture constitution

The terse normative rules that every part of OMNI must preserve:

authoritative state ownership;
principal and represented capacity;
consent and authority separation;
candidate versus commit;
projection versus authority;
correction and historical integrity;
admissibility before consequential action;
cross-boundary source preservation;
responsibility and custody continuity;
economic influence separation;
and the other laws that survive reconciliation.

This is where the word MUST belongs.

2. Reusable architecture patterns

Cross-domain compositions that recur but do not own truth themselves.

Likely candidates include:

evidence → verification → attributed meaning → adoption;
consequential intent → admissibility → commitment → consequence;
request/order → acceptance → fulfillment → proof;
governed external-principal participation;
obligation/custody continuity;
source-preserving projection;
versioned definition and policy;
correction-driven reopening;
governed capability exchange.

That is not a pre-approved list. The arc determines the real set.

3. Operating profiles

Concrete applications of several patterns at once.

An Insurance profile, Pharmacy profile, Laboratory profile, Gmail connector profile, or payroll profile does not invent its architecture. It declares:

inherits:
  - source_authority
  - candidate_not_commit
  - projection_not_authority
  - historical_integrity

instantiates:
  - governed_capability_exchange
  - external_principal_participation
  - obligation_continuity
  - source_preserving_projection

specializes:
  - coverage_relationship
  - funding_condition
  - determination_and_appeal
  - patient_responsibility

4. Conformance and compilation

The architecture must be enforceable through:

schemas;
compatibility checks;
seeded violations;
fixtures;

and Build Entry blockers.

A profile that cannot show which laws it inherited, how it specialized them, and how it proves compliance does not enter implementation.

It is not Reactor—but Reactor belongs inside it

The live Reactor terminus is clear about Reactor’s actual scope.

Reactor is the candidate intent-to-consequence constitution concerned with:

admissibility before consequence;
domain-owned commitment;
accepted custody;
no silent orphaning;
selective reopening;
compensation versus remedy versus reconsideration versus outcome;
honest projection;
bounded proof.

It is conceptually central and operationally distributed. It owns no domain state and must not become a reactor-service.

That is a major reusable architectural module.

It does not fully define:

evidence acquisition and clinical adoption;
longitudinal memory;
static truth ownership;
semantic reconciliation;
GCE crossing;
projection construction generally;
every definition/policy lifecycle;
agent runtime;
operating profiles;
or build conformance.

So:

Reactor is to the new architecture system what a powerful constitutional chapter is to a constitution—not the whole constitution and not a separate country.

The completed EVRUN‑000008 strengthened Reactor around cross-authority continuity, produced a 31/31-green conformance fixture, and left production/external proof as a separate maturity question.

The old closeout was right to prohibit endless Reactor essay-writing and a central Reactor object. It was wrong in practice to leave the module without an effective build-facing address.

Polaris, GCE, Reservoirs, maps, contracts: typed correctly

One reason this has remained vague is that several memorable OMNI concepts have been treated as though they are siblings when they are not the same artifact class.

Concept	Correct architectural role
Polaris	Alignment/orientation doctrine and computation: actor × relationship × authority × purpose × consent × context.
Reactor	Reusable consequential-transition and continuity pattern.
Reservoirs	Knowledge/evidence/memory substrate family.
GCE	Cross-boundary capability and exchange pattern.
System Map	Canonical map of P1 truth owners, domains, and seams.
Surface Map	Canonical map of P4 projections and P5 surfaces.
Domain contracts	Build-facing truth ownership, lifecycle, states, and verbs for a domain.
Profiles	Concrete compositions and specializations of multiple patterns and contracts.
Build OS	Retrieval, admission, construction, proof, and maintenance machinery.
Architecture control plane	Catalog, routing, authority, supersession, and discoverability—not architecture content.

The System Map itself says it is the P1 map, not doctrine, and that payloads such as Labs or Rx thread multiple loops and domains rather than becoming one domain.

The Surface Map says it is the P4/P5 peer of the System Map and owns no canonical truth.

Therefore, the missing thing is not simply a third map.

It is the parent architecture package that gives those maps and modules their relationship.

External sanity check

The general mechanism is established engineering practice.

FHIR separates a base specification from profiles and Implementation Guides; profiles can constrain inherited structures, define obligations, and cannot silently loosen obligations inherited from a base profile.

AWS applies a default architecture framework and allows one workload to carry multiple official or custom lenses, each with its own questions, best practices, and improvement plan.

AUTOSAR standardizes reusable application interfaces and exchanged semantics while deliberately leaving competitive application algorithms internal. That is the public automotive analogue to shared architecture plus specialized implementation.

Palantir’s Ontology similarly combines semantic types with governed actions and reusable interface-level action contracts. The substrate can represent and enforce an authored architecture, but it does not originate OMNI’s healthcare authority constitution for us.

So we are not inventing architecture reuse, profiles, or conformance.

We are authoring the OMNI-specific laws that those mechanisms must carry.

That's the forwards move and it's now Gate 1's first act. Fix the taxonomy — decide what classes of document exist and what authority each carries — *then* create artifacts. It's bounded, it needs no law reconciled first, and it's the thing you've been asking for since before insurance.

**On "constitution" — you're right, and the reason is architectural, not aesthetic.** A constitution is what everything rests on; in OMNI that's the thesis. This layer constrains construction and blocks non-conforming builds. So here are the established options with actual provenance, and you pick — no agent names this:

**specification** is the strongest for the normative core, because *conformance* is only meaningful against a specification — the word does the work. **Reference architecture** (SEI, Microsoft, AWS) is the strongest for the package that holds spec + patterns + profiles. **Base specification + profiles** is FHIR's, and it's the closest healthcare-native analogue — we've already half-inherited it through C4.6. **Architecture description** is ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010, the actual international standard for this exact artifact. *Building code* is the wrong domain but the right connotation: normative, testable, inspector-enforced, tells you what any building must satisfy without telling you what to build.

**On "patterns" — the honest answer is that it IS the established term.** Gang of Four, POSA, Fowler's *Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture*. It's diluted by overuse, not wrong. Inventing something better would be the eighth-label error. What matters more: our patterns carry conformance obligations, which makes them closer to FHIR profiles applied one level up than to a pattern catalogue.

**On Reactor — no, I don't trust that claim, and you don't need six gates to check it.** Knox says "Reactor is one module inside it" on the strength of the EVRUN terminus. But that terminus describes what the run was *chartered to answer* — intent-to-consequence continuity. It does not establish that Reactor is *only* that. Reactor's own framing is "candidate constitutional center," which is an ambition strictly larger than its evidenced scope. Reading "what the run covered" as "what the concept is" is a category error — and it's the same category error that produced everything else in this session.

It resolves in about an hour: lay Reactor's eight invariants beside Care's constitutional laws, GCE's crossing spine, and the 05-17 three-layer pattern, **in one table, once.** Either the eight cover the space or they visibly don't. That's a reading exercise in Gate 2, not a gate, not a pass, not another Reactor essay.

**On whether it's really four parts — no, probably six.** I pressure-tested Knox's four against ISO 42010 and against our own failure record, and two omissions are not cosmetic:

A **controlled vocabulary / term registry**. The seven-labels disease — one law carrying seven names across the estate — *is* a missing controlled vocabulary. No amount of pattern-writing fixes it. And **correspondence rules**, which is 42010's term for how the views relate to each other. Nothing in OMNI states how the System Map relates to the Surface Map relates to contracts relates to Reactor. **That absence is literally this session's disease** — every arc inferred the relationships and inferred them differently. Both are in the charter as parts 5 and 6, with Gate 2 deciding the final count.

**On your god-layer worry — it's the right worry and there's already a runnable guard.** The test is whether the package owns any truth or holds any commit authority. If no, it's a spec. If it starts owning state, it's a god layer wearing a spec's clothes. C4.6 `C10` — *no shadow god-domain, ownership matrix + schema review* — is that test and it already runs. I wired it into the charter as applying to this package itself, from the first commit, not as a later review.

**What I did, mechanically.** Knox is right about the package boundary and I'd repeated a defect the estate already recorded. Split done:

- **PR #15** — new branch off `main`, the FAI Gate-0 charter at R1 plus the two verbatim files and the handoff.
- **PR #14** — Insurance only now, frozen, `NOT ACCEPTED`, unmerged.

The two verbatim files are on the FAI branch and ready for you to paste into — markers are `<!-- BEGIN VERBATIM ... -->` / `<!-- END ... -->`. Their headers name the known-false claims they preserve on purpose, including my `EVRUN-000008` error, because the retractions are why the arc exists.

**One authorization is needed and nothing else.** Opening this changes the program's next action, which is checkpoint-level, and the integrator seat is vacant, so the checkpoint repoint, catalog rows and the read-graph route — including the load-bearing one that makes every future loop arc route *here* — are all written and all blocked. The line is in §11 of the charter if you want it verbatim: appoint me as integrator for the bounded arc-opening transaction only, not for Gate-1 authorship.

Zero shared surfaces touched. Nothing named, minted or promoted. `C3.9` and `E2` untouched.

Alignment

We are not choosing between OMNI Reactor and some newly invented super-layer.

The thing you are reaching for is simply:

OMNI Architecture

Not “OMNI Constitution.”
Not “OMNI Kernel.”
Not “OMNI Reference Architecture” as the master name.
Not “OMNI Architecture Description” as branding.
Not a new god-domain.

OMNI Architecture is the actual architecture of the company and system. The repository package that expresses it is its architecture description in the ISO sense. The reusable pieces inside it include standards, views, contracts, patterns, profiles, decisions, and conformance evidence.

That distinction finally gives Reactor a stable answer:

Reactor is not the whole of OMNI Architecture. Reactor is a named, cross-cutting architecture standard governing consequential transitions. It remains important, remains alive, and belongs inside OMNI Architecture.

This is not merely my interpretation of one tired closeout sentence. It follows from the scope of Reactor’s eight invariants: admissibility before consequence, domain-owned commitment, accepted custody, continuity, selective reopening, remedy distinctions, honest projection, and bounded proof. Those are profound rules governing intent becoming consequence. They do not define the entire domain map, evidence-adoption architecture, projection system, connector architecture, profile inheritance system, or artifact taxonomy.

The latest Opus reasoning is right to question whether we had overread the Reactor terminus, but wrong to leave Reactor’s role floating indefinitely. We now have enough evidence to classify its current architectural role without six more gates and without pretending its earlier ambition automatically controls.

We already had an architecture artifact system

The strongest correction to both Knox and Opus is this:

The repository already contains a Nick-and-Knox-ratified OMNI Architecture Artifact Index from the Foundation vNext pivot. It explicitly says:

OMNI did not lack an artifact OS; it had one, but its System Map and doctrine layers had drifted out of conformance.

It already defines these artifact roles:

System Map;
Domain Contract;
Seam/Event Contract;
Doctrine;
Decisions/ADRs;
Open Decisions;
Supersession;
Guardrails;
Field Cases;
Evidence/Workbenches;
Build OS;
Catalog and read routing.

It even calls domain contracts “the territory” and seam contracts the machine-checkable “glue between silos.”

So we are not discovering normal software architecture after six months from a blank page.

We are discovering that the existing artifact system:

was not kept current;
was not installed in a tool-independent home;
did not acquire several later-needed roles;
was not consistently routed;
and was not enforced against later arcs.

That is a narrower, more accurate diagnosis.

Opus’s taxonomy finding is only half right

The May 19 document taxonomy does not list contract, profile, pattern, specification, or conformance. It provides broad governance-handling categories such as doctrine, adr, evidence_or_ingestion, and handoff_or_readiness_gate.

Meanwhile, actual canonical files use artifact identities such as:

Document type: domain_contract

The D6 Commerce Contract is one live example.

But the conclusion is not:

“OMNI never understood contracts, so add contract to one flat category list.”

The Artifact Index already understood contracts.

The real defect is that OMNI has been conflating several different classification axes.

These must become separate fields
Axis	Question answered	Examples
Governance category	How is this artifact handled and routed?	doctrine, ADR, evidence, handoff
Architecture artifact role	What architectural job does it perform?	system map, domain contract, seam contract, architecture standard, profile
Authority/maturity	How strongly may it be relied upon?	candidate, draft, ratified, binding, superseded
Scope	Where does it apply?	universal, cross-cutting, domain, profile, deployment
Plane/view	What part of the architecture does it describe?	truth, seam, capability, projection, surface, runtime
Build/evidence maturity	Has it been implemented or externally demonstrated?	specified, fixture-tested, implemented, deployed, externally accepted

This is the taxonomy repair.

A document could therefore legitimately be:

governance_category: doctrine
architecture_role: cross_cutting_architecture_standard
authority: candidate_for_ratification
scope: cross_cutting
planes: [seam, capability, projection]
build_maturity: fixture_tested_partial

That is approximately Reactor’s honest current position.

This fixes the schema mismatch without cramming every architecture artifact into one giant category_enum.

The normal architecture vocabulary

Here is the clean terminology we should use.

Term	Meaning	OMNI use
Architecture	The fundamental structural and behavioral design of the actual system	OMNI Architecture
Architecture description	The set of artifacts that expresses the architecture	The full maps/contracts/standards/profiles/decisions package
Reference architecture	A reusable architectural baseline for a family of related implementations	Potentially useful for OMNI deployments or operator configurations—not the name of the whole company architecture
Architecture standard	Normative cross-cutting requirements: MUST/MUST NOT	Reactor, GCE, projection law, source-authority law
Pattern	A reusable solution to a recurring architectural problem, with context and tradeoffs	Saga, anti-corruption layer, evidence-to-adoption composition
Profile	A named specialization selecting and constraining the shared architecture for a context	Insurance, Pharmacy, Labs, Gmail, payroll
Contract	Build-facing semantics for an owned domain, interface, event, capability, projection, or surface	D6 contract, seam contract, GCE capability contract
View	A representation of the architecture addressing a particular concern	System Map, Surface Map, runtime/deployment view
ADR	The decision and rationale behind a consequential architectural choice	Existing ADRs and decision ledger
Conformance	Proof that a profile, contract, or implementation satisfies applicable requirements	C4.6 gates, Reactor fixture, future CI checks

This means “OMNI Reference Architecture” should not be the master name. A reference architecture is useful when defining a reusable baseline for a family of implementations. SEI describes it as an artifact for managing architectures that share common attributes and assets; that is related to OMNI’s multi-operator future, but it is not identical to the actual architecture of OMNI itself.

The master name is already available and does not need branding:

OMNI Architecture

Named concepts such as Polaris, Reactor, Reservoirs, and GCE remain memorable mechanisms inside it.

“Constitution” should be removed—but not because the thesis is literally a constitution

Your discomfort is right. The reason needs sharpening.

The Thesis states what OMNI is, why it exists, the strategic and care worldview, and what business/system it intends to become.
Doctrine and architecture standards state binding invariants.
Architecture structurally realizes the thesis under those invariants.
Contracts make the architecture buildable.
Profiles specialize it.
Conformance proves it.

Calling the new package a “constitution” blurs thesis, doctrine, authority, and architecture into one metaphor. That is exactly the kind of semantic overloading we are trying to eliminate.

So:

constitution.md        → reject
OMNI Constitution      → reject

We need no substitute branded term.

ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010: use it, but do not become it

ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010:2022 is directly relevant—but it does not tell us what OMNI’s architecture must be or which folders to create.

The standard:

distinguishes an architecture from the architecture description expressing it;
applies to software, systems, enterprises, product lines, technologies, and business domains;
specifies concepts for architecture descriptions, frameworks, viewpoints, views, and model kinds;
and explicitly does not prescribe the architecture itself, architecting process, notation, tool, file format, or recording medium.

Therefore:

OMNI should be 42010-informed during this arc, not presently claim 42010 conformance.

Use it as a completeness and consistency lens:

What is the entity of interest?
Who are the stakeholders?
What concerns must the architecture address?
Which viewpoints exist?
Which views answer those concerns?
Which model kinds are used?
What correspondences connect the views?
Are contradictions visible?

Do not:

call the package “OMNI Architecture Description”;
copy ISO vocabulary into OMNI merely because it is standardized;
claim compliance without evaluating the complete standard;
or expect ISO 42010 to provide OMNI’s healthcare laws.

“Architecture description” can appear in metadata as the technical name for the artifact collection. It is not the product name.

FHIR is a mechanism analogue, not OMNI’s identity

FHIR profiling provides useful mechanics:

a canonical identifier;
explicit versioning;
a base definition;
constrained specialization;
status and publisher;
machine-readable differentials and snapshots;
and validation/tooling against the declared profile.

FHIR’s StructureDefinition is specifically for describing data structures and constraints and supporting comparison, code generation, reports, and UI generation. Profiles can constrain a base resource or another profile.

OMNI profiles are broader. They must govern:

authority;
ownership;
consent;
commitments;
custody;
correction;
workflows;
projections;
experience;
and conformance.

So:

Borrow FHIR’s inheritance, versioning, differential, and validation mechanics. Do not describe OMNI as “building our own FHIR.”

The artifact should use the term Operating Profile or Architecture Profile so future agents do not mistake it for a FHIR resource profile.

Palantir also gives us a useful mechanism—but not the package name

Palantir uses Interfaces as abstract types describing shared shape and capabilities. Concrete object types may implement multiple interfaces, inheriting required properties, link constraints, and action capabilities. Workflows can operate through the interface rather than knowing every concrete type.

That is a strong implementation analogue for how OMNI profiles or reusable contracts could work:

shared requirements
+ required capabilities
+ permitted specialization
+ multiple implementation
+ conformance declaration

But Palantir’s Ontology is an operational semantic layer over organizational data and actions. It is not an architecture-document taxonomy and is not the right name for what we are building.

Reactor: the final aligned answer
Reactor is neither dead nor the whole thing

Reactor should currently be classified as:

a named cross-cutting OMNI architecture standard for consequential transitions and cross-authority continuity.

Its scope is:

consequential intent
→ admissibility
→ owning-domain commitment
→ accepted custody
→ honest continuity
→ selective reopening
→ remedy / reconsideration / outcome separation
→ bounded proof

Its relationship to the larger architecture is:

Concern	Reactor owns the architectural standard?
Consequential intent becoming real-world effect	Yes
Admissibility before consequence	Yes
Accepted custody and no silent orphaning	Yes
Selective reopening and remedy distinctions	Yes
Complete domain/truth ownership map	No — System Map and contracts
Evidence verification and clinical adoption	No — Reservoirs/Observation/CM/D7 architecture
Universal cross-boundary capability exchange	No — GCE
All projections and surfaces	No — Surface Map and projection contracts
Profile inheritance and variance	No — missing profile system
Architecture artifact taxonomy	No — Artifact Index/governance
Thesis, mission, and company strategy	No — Thesis
Build/runtime agent system	No — Build OS and Agent Runtime

This is not an insult or demotion. It is how Reactor becomes usable rather than mystical.

Its prior evidence remains valid for that scope. Broadening it into the entire architecture would silently claim evidence for questions the Reactor runs never tested. That would be the dangerous move.

The Gate‑2 reconciliation should test whether Reactor’s standard has adjacent clauses elsewhere and whether any of its eight invariants need promotion, narrowing, or deduplication. It should not reopen Reactor’s identity from zero.

Knox’s four parts are not the complete taxonomy

The four items—

architecture rules;
reusable patterns;
profiles;
conformance—

describe four capabilities the missing system needs.

They are not a complete architecture artifact model.

Opus’s proposed additions—controlled vocabulary and correspondence rules—are important, but they are not necessarily two equal sibling “parts” either.

A credible OMNI Architecture package currently appears to need these artifact roles:

Architecture entrypoint and scope
What OMNI Architecture contains, authority hierarchy, artifact roles, and maintenance rules.
Architecture standards
Normative cross-cutting requirements. Reactor and GCE likely land here after authority reconciliation.
Views and maps
System, surface, runtime, deployment, trust/authority, information, operating views.
Contracts and interfaces
Domain, seam/event, capability, projection, and surface contracts.
Reusable patterns
Contextual solution patterns with applicability and consequences—not a junk drawer for every recurring phrase.
Operating profiles
Insurance, Pharmacy, Labs, connector, deployment, and operator specializations.
Decisions and rationale
ADRs and decision records.
Conformance and evaluation
Requirements-to-test mapping, fixtures, seeded failures, CI evidence, implementation state.
Controlled vocabulary
Canonical terms, aliases, deprecated terms, concept ownership.
Traceability and correspondence
Exact relationships among thesis → standard → view → contract → profile → implementation → proof.

Those ten roles do not necessarily mean ten folders or ten Markdown files. Some are structured metadata; some are collections; some already exist.

Gate 2 determines the final artifact model. It should not begin from “four is correct” or “six is correct.”

The final repository shape

The final architecture must be tool-independent and root-discoverable.

A credible starting shape is:

/architecture
  README.md                    # authoritative entrypoint and artifact model

  /standards                   # normative cross-cutting rules
    reactor.md
    governed-capability-exchange.md
    source-authority.md
    projection-authority.md

  /views                       # maps / viewpoints
    system.md
    surfaces.md
    runtime.md
    trust-authority.md
    deployment.md

  /contracts
    /domains
    /seams
    /capabilities
    /projections
    /surfaces

  /profiles
    pharmacy.md
    mixed-financing.md
    labs-diagnostics.md
    /connectors
      gmail.md
      slack.md
      payroll.md
      banking.md

  /patterns                    # only actual reusable solution patterns

  /decisions                   # ADRs or pointers to canonical ADRs

  /vocabulary

  /conformance                 # requirements, fixtures, test mappings

This is a proposed physical model, not yet the final locked tree.

Two immediate constraints:

Do not create constitution.md.
Do not automatically create manifest.yaml.

The existing catalog and read graph already act as manifests. A second hand-maintained manifest could recreate the duplicate-state failure. A machine-readable architecture manifest is valuable only if it becomes the single source or is generated automatically from canonical metadata.

Likewise, do not throw Reactor, GCE, source authority, sagas, and every recurring idea into one /patterns folder. Reactor and GCE are likely standards; sagas and anti-corruption layers are patterns. The distinction matters.

What PR #15 still gets wrong

PR #15 is directionally sound, but its current R1 charter is not ready for acceptance.

1. It overlooks the existing Artifact Index

The charter frames the absent contract value in the May category enum as though OMNI lacked a contract class. The ratified Architecture Artifact Index already defines Domain Contracts and Seam Contracts.

Correct diagnosis:

Governance category taxonomy and architecture artifact-role taxonomy are misaligned.

Not:

“OMNI never classified contracts.”

2. It still leaves Reactor artificially unsettled

The charter says Reactor’s scope is unresolved because its ambition exceeded its tested scope.

Its ambition may be unresolved. Its current evidence-supported architectural role is not:

consequential-transition architecture standard.

That should be the starting classification. Gate 2 can broaden only through an explicit decision with evidence.

3. It treats “patterns” too generously

“Pattern” is an established term. It is not the correct class for every recurring OMNI law.

The charter must distinguish:

standard / invariant
pattern
profile
contract
view
4. It overstates the role of ISO 42010

42010 should inform the architecture description and correspondence model. It should not be presented as a candidate name or copied artifact taxonomy.

5. Gate 1 should not begin by editing the old flat category enum

Gate 1 should:

install the tool-independent architecture root;
establish the multi-axis artifact model;
reconcile the existing Artifact Index into it;
then update governance schemas so they can represent the installed architecture correctly.

Architecture first; governance schema follows the installed architecture—not the reverse.

## Assistant

Your sequencing instinct is right, and the reason is now visible: **the taxonomy *is* the stake.** They're not two moves.

The evidence is this session. The moment the question became "what artifact classes exist," it produced more build-relevant clarity in one pass than five arcs produced in months. That's not luck — taxonomy is the *container* question, and containers constrain everything you put in them. Insurance, Pharmacy and Care each spent an arc discovering they had nowhere to put what they found.

And it explains why your original plan kept failing. Spine → thesis → taxonomy died five times because **a spine is a statement of an architecture, and we kept trying to state one that had never been organized.** Corrected order: organize, then state, then explain. Contracts already exist; they get reconciled in, not rebuilt.

**The name is `OMNI Architecture`, and you're right that it sounds like nothing special — that's the point.** It's not a coinage because it's not an invention; it's the thing we've been building unlabelled for six months. "OMNI Reference Architecture" is out for exactly the reason you said out loud: a *reference architecture* is a reusable baseline for a **family of implementations** — which is a real and useful part of the 1000-deployment problem, but it is a part, not the whole. Constitution is out, and there's a hard reason beyond taste: **the Artifact Index already uses "constitutional invariants" for Doctrine.** The word is taken.

**On FHIR and 42010 muddying future-us — here's the one-line rule I put in the charter.** We borrow FHIR's *mechanics*: canonical identifier, explicit versioning, a base that a specialization constrains, differential vs snapshot, validation against a declared profile, and the rule that a specialization **may constrain but may never loosen** what it inherits. We reject the *identity* — a FHIR profile constrains a data structure; ours governs authority, consent, custody, correction and conformance. So the artifact is an **Operating Profile**, never an unqualified "profile," so nobody in six months thinks it's a StructureDefinition. 42010 is a **completeness lens** — what's the entity, who are the stakeholders, which viewpoints, which views, what correspondences, where are the contradictions — used during the arc and never claimed as conformance, never adopted as vocabulary, never the name. Your instinct was no, and no is right.

**Reactor — here is the straight answer, and I'll own that I was the one keeping it vague.**

> **Reactor is a candidate cross-cutting architecture *standard* governing consequential transitions and cross-authority continuity. Not dead. Not the whole thing. Not "unsettled."**

I refused this last round on the grounds that the EVRUN terminus describes what the run was *chartered* to answer rather than what the concept *is*. That reasoning was correct and the consequence was wrong — **leaving the role floating "until reconciliation" is exactly what kept Reactor unfindable for three weeks and three arcs.** Classify at evidenced scope now; Gate 2 can broaden it by explicit decision with evidence. A revisable classification beats an honest vacancy. That was my error and it cost a round.

**On the taxonomy, I was half wrong and Knox caught it.** There isn't one taxonomy — there are **two, and they're mutually invisible.** The governance enum (10 categories, no `contract`, while 16 contracts exist) and the ratified `00_architecture_artifact_index.md` (12 architecture roles — and verified absent: `standard`, `pattern`, `operating profile`, `conformance`, `vocabulary`, and any `view` beyond the System Map). So it's a schema mismatch plus a stale role set, not an absence. The repair is six independent axes rather than one flat enum — and note what that buys: **Reactor's honest position is only expressible across all six at once, which is precisely why it has been unclassifiable and therefore unfindable.** The classification failure and the discovery failure are the same failure.

**Now the four things you raised that neither Knox nor I had, and these are the most valuable part of your message.**

**"This isn't one version of Hims, it's 1000." — there are two profile axes and conflating them would be fatal.** *Operating-area* profiles (Insurance, Pharmacy, Gmail, payroll) and *deployment* profiles (single clinic, federation, enterprise). They're orthogonal — Henry Ford's instance runs an operating profile **and** a deployment profile. Knox's ten roles and my six parts both only had the first one. The estate already has the deployment vocabulary sitting homeless in the pre-spine map §5: OMNI-primary, OMNI-composed-enterprise, OMNI-federated-network-node.

**"Henry Ford says conform it to us" — the answer is variation points, and it's the difference between scaling to 1000 and dying at 20.** The architecture declares *in advance* where deviation is permitted. Inside a declared variation point, it's **configuration**. Outside it, it's a **change to the architecture** and goes through the architecture's own process — not a customer's ticket. Without that, every enterprise customer negotiates against the whole architecture and the architecture loses every time. This is the SEI product-line mechanism, and SEI names four failure modes of unmanaged variability — duplicate mechanisms, incompatible variation choices, unnecessary variation, missed required variations — **all four of which are already observable in this estate.**

**"How does an agent see one federation, all federations, OMNI at 100k feet" — that's a viewpoint question, and both our existing maps are builder-facing.** Instance view and fleet view don't exist. The reader isn't only a builder; it's an agent operating one deployment and an agent operating the estate.

**"How do changes get made to the architecture, really to the repo as a whole" — currently nowhere, and it's a Gate-1 deliverable, not a nicety.** We have fragments — Build Entry, AWP §5, the supersession ledger, the catalog — and nothing that says how an architecture change is raised, evaluated, accepted, rejected or superseded, or who may. **A maintained architecture without a change process becomes the 05-17 pattern: universally routed and quietly stale.** That's the mechanism that would have prevented every staleness failure we found this week.

All four are in the R2 charter, pushed to **PR #15**. Insurance stays frozen at PR #14.

**On the veer.** It's real and I won't dress it up — you drove four rounds of review to prove a gate was failing, and what it exposed was that the container was missing, not that insurance was hard. The one thing I'd push back on is "all because insurance failed us." Insurance didn't fail — it was the first arc that pressed hard enough on enough domains that the missing container became undeniable. Pharmacy nearly did it and got absorbed. That's worth something, and it's why insurance should return as the first profile proof rather than being restarted from scratch.

One authorization still blocks the arc from opening: the integrator seat is vacant and the checkpoint repoint is checkpoint-level. Exact line is in §13 of the charter — bounded to the arc-opening transaction, not Gate-1 authorship. Nothing auto-starts without it.

## Assistant

Both your objections were right and I restructured Knox's arc around them. Pushed to PR #15.

**On where the external reconciliation happens — Knox had it at G5, which is backwards, and it's the same mistake that caused all this.** His order was: recover the whole estate, synthesize OMNI's architecture, build the profiles, *then* check it against ISO 42010, SEI, FHIR, IHE, AUTOSAR, AWS, Palantir. That means spending the entire synthesis budget deriving an artifact-role model out of our own history and *then* discovering we built a worse version of a solved problem. It's literally the failure we already diagnosed — **we carried FHIR in the comparator registry for months as a payload standard and never as a method.** Putting the method comparison last repeats it.

So it moved to first. It's the cheapest thing in the whole arc — a handful of primary sources, days not weeks — and its output *is* the artifact-role model and the variation model that everything downstream classifies into. You don't invent the role taxonomy from six months of scar tissue and then audit it. You take the one that exists, map it onto what we have, and note where healthcare forces a difference.

**On insurance-as-qualifier — you're right and it's a category error, so I cut it.** Profile pressure proves the architecture can *express* Insurance. It proves nothing about whether the documents are in the right place and findable, which is the actual failure. And you're right that an agent will happily write convincing prose that Insurance is well-modelled while the estate stays unnavigable.

The replacement is the test that was already sitting in both of our closing lines without either of us promoting it: **a cold agent entering Insurance, Pharmacy, Gmail, payroll or a new federation gets routed to the right architecture, profiles, variation points and proof obligations — with no historical filename, no arc reading, no access to any of this.** That's mechanically checkable with a fixture, it fails loudly, and it can run early instead of at the end. Profile declarations still get written, but as proof the *declaration format* carries authority and inheritance — not as proof the domains are right.

**And the consequence you'll care about most: the arc got roughly half as big.** Knox's G2 pays the whole-estate synthesis tax up front, before anything is installed. That's the big bang, and it's precisely why five arcs' findings evaporated — there was nowhere to put them. Inverted: install the container, then **classify** existing artifacts into it *in place* — role, authority, maturity, home, conflicts — without rewriting a single one. That's cheap and mechanical. Deep reconciliation then happens per area, when that area is next touched, because a home finally exists. Five gates instead of eight. And Knox's G5 market/incumbent pressure is deferred with its destination named — Task-D and the spine already own it, and running it here would be the third re-derivation of the same comparator material.

**Your LangGraph/IBM question deserves a straight answer and it's deflating: they do considerably less than this.** A `docs/architecture` directory, ADRs, a README that says what the system is, and a rule that changes go through it. **Most teams have less material than we have.** What they have that we don't is one obvious entry point and an enforced change path. That's the entire gap. It isn't exotic, it isn't a research problem, and you're right that it could have been done in week 4 — the reason it wasn't is that every arc had somewhere to *write* and nowhere to *file*, so each one filed into itself.

Knox's two byte defects are fixed — the handoff still said "the single-law outpost" after that probe was deleted, and still said rejecting the charter unfreezes Insurance. It doesn't; the arc is decided, rejection means revise the plan.

I also wired the method repertoire in properly rather than ignoring it — it's real, 80 methods, and it's now a mandatory *consult* with every individual method *optional*, plus a per-gate matrix that forces each choice to record why it was selected and what was rejected. That's the difference between using it and performing it.

Two files on PR #15 now: the charter (R3, the *why*) and the execution plan (the *how* the next agent runs, without redesigning it). Still no integrator appointment requested — Knox is right that it waits for this review. Insurance frozen, `C3.9` and `E2` untouched, nothing named.

The part R3 still under-specifies:

Capability

What it must do

Architecture catalog/graph

Maintain IDs, owners, versions, roles, dependencies, applicability, supersession, and proof links; generated from canonical source rather than becoming another copy

Change proposal system

Impact analysis

Traverse standard → profile → contract → code/config → deployment → test relationships before change approval

Architecture compiler

Conformance engine

Test inherited requirements, forbidden loosening, source/commit authority, profile compatibility, and implementation adherence

Propagation engine

Generate or propose updates to contracts, templates, code, policies, tests, migrations, and deployment configuration

Fleet reconciliation

Know which deployments run which architecture/profile versions; plan upgrades, skew windows, deprecations, and exceptions

Architecture observability

Compare declared architecture to code, configuration, deployment, and runtime behavior; detect drift and stale exceptions

Agentic workbench

Let bounded research, impact, domain, migration, conformance, release, and monitoring agents cooperate without gaining universal authority

Exception/debt lifecycle

Record approved deviation, owner, scope, expiry, compensating controls, and required removal or promotion


The architecture content says what must be true.

Architecture operations make it stay true.

        │
        ▼

        │
        ▼
9. Release/fleet agents

        │
        ▼

    compare intended and live state; open drift proposals, never silently rewrite

The acceptance test must be broader than routing

Cold routing stays.

It becomes one part of an end-to-end test suite.

Test

Question

Routing

Can a fresh agent find the right architecture without historical knowledge?

Applicability resolution

Can it determine the exact standards, profile versions, deployment posture, and exceptions that apply here?

Impact

If one standard changes, can the system enumerate all affected profiles, contracts, code, tests, deployments, and owners?

Parallel change

Can two agents propose overlapping changes without silent overwrite or duplicated architecture?

Authority

Can agents propose broadly while only rightful owners approve and commit?

Propagation

Does an approved change produce or request every required downstream update?

Conformance

Does a profile loosening an inherited rule fail? Does unauthorized truth ownership fail?

Fleet

Can small-operator, composed-enterprise, and federated-node deployments resolve different effective snapshots without forking the architecture?

Drift

Does the system detect code, configuration, deployment, or runtime behavior that no longer conforms?

Upgrade/rollback

Can architecture versions move forward, coexist temporarily, deprecate, and roll back with explicit rules?

Insurance, Pharmacy, Gmail, payroll, and a non-cousin remain valuable fixtures.

They are not the sole acceptance criterion.

⸻

The remaining 10%

1. Separate the three machine-readable objects

R4 currently says:

* JSON Schema “manifest”;
* Backstage catalog format;
* generated catalog/graph;
* no hand-maintained manifest duplicating the catalog.

Those ideas are individually reasonable but still ambiguous together. They can easily produce two or three competing metadata sources.

The installed system needs three distinct objects:

architecture resource descriptor
    describes one standard, view, contract, profile, pattern, decision,
    vocabulary, or conformance suite

work-package manifest
    describes one bounded build/change operation, its claims, writers,
    branches, inputs, outputs, reviewers, and stops

effective-architecture snapshot
    generated resolution of the architecture that applies to one logical
    deployment/operator/federation at one version


Required single-source rule

canonical architecture resource descriptors
        │
        ├──► generated architecture graph/catalog
        ├──► generated Backstage-compatible entities
        ├──► impact analysis
        └──► effective-architecture compiler

work-package manifests are separate Build-OS execution objects.
They are never the architecture catalog.

Use JSON Schema to validate both descriptor classes, but use different schemas. JSON Schema validates document structure and constraints; cross-resource compatibility and graph semantics require additional policy and graph checks. 

Backstage decision

Borrow:

* the entity envelope;
* stable references;
* relation processing;
* source-controlled descriptors;
* extensibility;
* optional future portal.

Do not adopt Backstage’s native entity taxonomy or spec.owner semantics as OMNI authority. Backstage’s documentation explicitly describes many owner fields as responsibility/display metadata rather than runtime authorization, and its relations are commonly derived by processors rather than manually copied into every descriptor. 

The decision should therefore read:

Adopt a Backstage-compatible OMNI resource-descriptor envelope with OMNI-defined kinds and relations. Canonical OMNI descriptors remain the source. A Backstage catalog is a generated consumer and future UI—not the authority model.

That is better than “adopt the Backstage catalog format” without qualification.

⸻

2. CODEOWNERS does not implement ownership leases

R4 currently maps:


ownership leases + shared-surface locks
→ CODEOWNERS + branch protection


That is false.

CODEOWNERS can:

* request reviews;
* identify responsible users or teams;
* participate in protected-branch approval requirements.

Branch protection and rulesets can require reviews, status checks, conversation resolution, and merge queues. 

They do not provide:

* an active work lease;
* temporary exclusive ownership of a resource;
* lease expiry;
* transfer;
* overlapping-claim detection;
* or an enforceable “this agent currently holds this architecture resource.”

The existing CODEOWNERS file is also materially stale for this purpose: it points at the legacy system map, covers selected old paths, and names one owner. It has no future /architecture package, profile, standard, or deployment-model coverage.

Correct mechanism

Adopt:

CODEOWNERS + repository rulesets + required checks + merge queue
    = approval and merge control

architecture_change.yaml / work-package manifest resource claims
    = active ownership lease and collision control


A change claim should minimally contain:


change_id:
principal:
owner:
branch:
base_ref:
claimed_resources:
  - resource_id:
    mode: exclusive | coordinated
lease_expires_at:
required_reviewers:
integration_path:
state:



CI must reject:

* overlapping exclusive claims;
* expired claims;
* a branch touching undeclared resources;
* a proposal merging without required resource-owner review;
* direct edits to protected generated surfaces.

That is the thin, real version of the Build OS lease target.

⸻

3. The effective-architecture compiler is the center of the 1000-instance model

R4 names an “effective-architecture compiler,” but does not yet give it an output contract.

This is not a secondary utility. It is the thing that prevents “1000 versions of Hims” from becoming 1000 architecture forks.

Its computation is:

OMNI Architecture release
+ applicable architecture standards
+ operating-area profiles
+ deployment profile / reference architecture
+ federation/operator/tenant variation selections
+ approved exceptions
+ compatibility and deprecation rules
──────────────────────────────────────────────
effective architecture snapshot


The result must be:

* deterministic;
* version-pinned;
* source-linked;
* hashable;
* reconstructable as-of;
* compatibility-checked;
* explicit about unresolved conflicts;
* explicit about approved exceptions and expiry;
* approved by the relevant owners;
* and itself a projection, never source truth.

Minimum output:


architecture_release:
standards:
operating_profiles:
deployment_profile:
federation_operator_scope:
variation_selections:
approved_exceptions:
effective_requirements:
required_contracts:
required_conformance:
compatibility_result:
source_manifest:
generated_at:
content_hash:


One crucial distinction

Do not equate:

logical OMNI instance / operator / federation profile


with:

physical software deployment

OMNI may serve thousands of operators through:

* one multi-tenant deployment;
* several regional deployments;
* dedicated enterprise installations;
* hybrid or federated nodes.

The logical fleet exists before Kubernetes, Argo, or separate deployments exist.

Fleet reconciliation must therefore be designed now, independently of the eventual infrastructure orchestrator.

⸻

4. Architecture Operations must not become a new god-layer

R4’s “Architecture Operations” is correct as a capability family.

It must not become a new owner of everything.

The capability ownership must be explicit:


Capability

Existing rightful owner

Architecture standards, contracts, profiles, views

OMNI Architecture package and their declared owners

Classification, catalog routing, authority, supersession

Architecture Memory Control Plane

Change proposals, claims, protected writes, integration

Build OS

Agent definitions, runtime profiles, sessions, tools, delegation

Agent Runtime

Domain semantics and commits

Each owning domain

Release, physical deployment, fleet rollout

Release/Runtime + deployment infrastructure

Federation/operator applicability

Federation + deployment profile

Runtime evidence and telemetry

Runtime/E&V under the applicable contracts

Cross-cutting acceptance

Architecture steward/review gate, not a universal runtime object

So the durable rule is:

OMNI Architecture Operations composes existing owners into a lifecycle. It does not own architecture truth, domain truth, runtime truth, deployment truth, or agent authority.

Add that sentence to the plan.

5. Propagation v0 should generate obligations before it rewrites code

R4 names a propagation engine and defers OpenRewrite until the first change requiring ten or more mechanical edits.

Two corrections:

The first propagation engine is an impact-and-obligation generator

Version 0 should:

* identify affected artifacts;
* create required downstream-change obligations;
* assign owners;
* block closure until each obligation is completed, explicitly deferred, or shown not applicable;
* regenerate only truly generated artifacts.

It should not silently rewrite semantic contracts or code.

“Ten edits” is the wrong trigger

The trigger is:

a repeatable, mechanically specifiable semantic transformation with a decisive verifier

—not an arbitrary edit count.

A two-file change can be high-risk and worth a recipe. A fifty-file change can be too semantically ambiguous to automate safely.

Also, OpenRewrite’s current open-source core is strongest in Java/Kotlin/Groovy and structured formats; JavaScript/TypeScript recipes rely on the Moderne CLI and include source-available components. That makes it a possible future cross-repository transformation system, but not the obvious default for this TypeScript-first codebase. 

The decision should be:

Use stack-native TypeScript codemods first. Evaluate OpenRewrite/Moderne when OMNI has repeatable polyglot or cross-repository migrations whose scale justifies it.

Argo CD should remain conditional on the eventual deployment substrate. Do not select a Kubernetes reconciler merely because “fleet” exists.

⸻

6. OpenTelemetry is the evidence convention, not the drift engine

Adopting OpenTelemetry conventions is sensible.

But OpenTelemetry supplies common semantics for traces, metrics, logs, profiles, and resources. It does not determine whether OMNI conforms to its architecture. 

The architecture should define an OMNI telemetry envelope such as:


omni.architecture.version
omni.operating_profile.ids
omni.deployment_profile.id
omni.federation.id
omni.operator.id
omni.policy_decision.id
omni.capability.id
omni.represented_principal.kind
omni.commit_owner
omni.conformance.result


But:

* do not place PHI or raw patient context into these attributes;
* use scoped identifiers;
* classify high-cardinality or sensitive attributes;
* make sensitive values opt-in or forbidden.

OpenTelemetry’s own conventions call for warnings and minimization around sensitive information. 

So:

OpenTelemetry = runtime evidence transport and vocabulary

OMNI conformance engine = decides whether that evidence demonstrates
or contradicts the architecture

Keep those separate.

⸻

7. The multi-agent loop describes functions, not ten mandatory agents

R4’s multi-agent loop is useful:

evidence → classification → proposal → impact → review
→ conformance → migration → integration → fleet → observation



But these must be functional roles, not a compulsory ten-agent pipeline.

One agent may perform several compatible functions in a low-risk change.

Hard separation is required only where independence or authority demands it:

* proposer cannot approve its own cross-cutting proposal;
* migration agent cannot waive failed conformance;
* observer cannot silently repair live drift;
* adversary/adjudicator independence is required only at the gates that call for it;
* domain owners retain approval over their own resources.

Each function should emit a typed result:


Function

Typed output

Evidence

source receipt

Classification

terminus/authority/classification result

Proposal

architecture change proposal

Impact

affected-resource report

Review

owner decision

Conformance

conformance report

Migration

patch + migration proof

Integration

merge/landing receipt

Fleet

rollout/effective-snapshot record

Observation

drift finding / proposed remediation


That lets one context perform multiple roles without losing the chain.

It avoids turning your request for multi-agent readiness into another mandatory-agent ceremony.

At this stage, they can prove:


architecture_operations_v0

* production deployment reconciliation;
* runtime care-agent behavior;

runtime_and_fleet_proof

Do not allow the first receipt to be read as the second.

This preserves the installation-versus-evidence maturity distinction that opened the arc in the first place.

## Assistant

R5/R3 is pushed. Knox's ten patches are all in, and I did one of them harder than asked.

**The charter's duplicate gate block is deleted, not refreshed.** Knox asked me to update it; I removed it. It had already drifted inside a single revision — still describing external-first ordering and routing-as-acceptance after both were superseded. `D0CKPT-GRD-004` says refreshing a stale duplicate preserves the mechanism, and that guardrail was earned two days ago on exactly this failure. There is now one gate sequence, in the execution plan, and the charter points at it.

The two mechanics corrections that mattered most were both places I'd been imprecise. **`CODEOWNERS` is not an ownership lease** — it requests reviews and gates merges; it has no exclusivity, expiry, transfer or overlap detection. Those are now two separate rows with two separate mechanisms. And the **OpenRewrite trigger was wrong** — "ten edits" is an arbitrary count; the real trigger is a repeatable, mechanically specifiable transformation with a decisive verifier. A two-file change can deserve a recipe and a fifty-file change can be too ambiguous to automate safely.

I also withdrew the Palantir line. "Not ahead of us on any of that" was more certainty than the work supports — we've established that an ontology platform doesn't by itself supply the healthcare constitution, not that Palantir fails to.

**Your three points are in, and the second one is the sharpest thing anyone has said about our Build OS.**

The prior inputs are named and mandatory now, not gestured at: six AI-corpus concept registries with routing maps — `EVRUN-000001/2/3/5/6/11` — plus the federation permeability arc. Those registries are the distilled form of the 300+ ingests and they're the right consumption unit; the raws stay closed. The rule is that anything called new has to fail `M-106` EXISTS-AS against those six *first*. An arc that re-derives Build OS concepts the corpus already routed has failed before it starts.

And your critique is correct: **Step-5's targets are competent 2020s platform practice.** Manifests, validators, leases, merge queues, policy-as-code — that's what a good team builds today. It is not an agent-native operating model for 2030–2035, and no arc has ever consumed those registries for operations design. So G1 now runs the model against two bars, and the second one is the real one: *what does this design assume that stops being true when a thousand agents a day propose changes, when review capacity is the bottleneck instead of authoring, when drift is continuous instead of episodic, and when the reader of the architecture is more often a machine than a person?* Anything that only clears current practice gets marked `current_practice_only` with the gap named. That's the bean sprout, and now it's labelled as one.

**The pluggability rule stopped being a promise and became test 11.** Remove every third-party tool and the architecture must still resolve and every law must still be stated and checkable. Tools can make conformance fast and automatic; none of them can be the place a rule lives. A rule that only exists inside a vendor's format is already surrendered. That's the DNA test, it's mechanical, and it means nobody has to write that paragraph again.

On the oak tree — the part that has to be right at planting is narrow, and I think it's these four: the laws, the ability to resolve which of them apply here, the ability to change them safely and propagate the change, and the ability to detect when reality has diverged. Content will be rewritten many times. Tools will be swapped. Deployments will multiply. Those four are what has to be substrate-independent on day one, because they're the only things you can't retrofit later without rewriting everything built on top of them.

Conceptually converged. What's left is byte review, G0 acceptance, the bounded integrator appointment, then G1 executes. Insurance still frozen at PR #14, `C3.9` and `E2` untouched.
