The current R5/R3 direction is strong. It has finally inherited the frontier registries, separated architecture content from architecture operations, made tool independence testable, and stopped pretending Build OS is being invented from scratch. PR #15 remains open, draft, and unmerged at head fb23710…; no shared control-plane surface has landed.

But you identified two real omissions:

1. The “oak-tree DNA” is still only conversational compression. It has no declared durable home.
2. The arc has no fresh-context counter-design of the full 2030/2035 OMNI Architecture question.

Those are worth fixing. They do not justify another redesign.

⸻

Yes, write the four things down

But they are not four new care laws.

They are not:

* thesis prose alone;
* a domain contract;
* a Build OS-only protocol;
* Reactor’s next four invariants;
* or another universal-doctrine list.

They are the root requirements of OMNI Architecture as a maintained system.

The clean formulation is:

Root requirements of OMNI Architecture

1. Explicit
    Every binding architectural requirement exists in an OMNI-owned, substrate-independent canonical form. No vendor, tool, conversation, implementation detail, or human recollection is the only place a rule exists.
2. Resolvable
    For any mission, operator, federation, tenant, deployment posture, agent, and point in time, OMNI can deterministically resolve the exact architecture, standards, profiles, variations, exceptions, owners, and proof obligations that apply.
3. Evolvable
    An architectural change can be proposed, authority-checked, impact-analyzed, reviewed, versioned, propagated, migrated, coexisted, deprecated, and reversed without silently forking the architecture or losing history.
4. Observable
    OMNI can compare declared architecture with artifacts, code, configuration, effective deployment state, and runtime evidence; detect divergence; attribute it; and open a governed correction path.

A simpler mnemonic is:

State it.
Resolve it.
Change it safely.
Know when reality diverges.

That mnemonic is not a new branded doctrine. It is just the readable compression.

Where it belongs

The exact four-line normative block belongs in the eventual:

/architecture/README.md

under a section such as:

Root requirements

The detailed clauses belong in the Architecture Operations standard or contract created by G2. Their tests belong in the architecture conformance suite.

The ownership split is:



Artifact

Relationship to the four requirements

OMNI Architecture entrypoint

Owns the compact normative statement

Architecture standards/operations contract

Owns the detailed obligations

Conformance suite

Proves them

Build OS

Executes the change and proof mechanics

Agent Runtime

Applies them to agent runs

Spine

Explains their place in the integrated system

Thesis

Explains why they matter to OMNI’s mission and strategy

Domain contracts and profiles

Compile them locally without restating them

So the answer to your question is precise:

They are candidate cross-cutting architecture-system requirements. Preserve them immediately as a required G2 deliverable. Ratify them only after G1/G3 reconciliation and G4 proof.

That prevents both failure modes:

* letting them evaporate because they appeared in chat;
* prematurely declaring four eloquent sentences to be universal doctrine.

R5’s current plan contains the machinery corresponding to these ideas—catalog and graph, effective-architecture compiler, proposal and impact flow, propagation, fleet reconciliation, observability, and conformance—but it does not yet preserve the four as the system’s compact root contract.

And yes: the fact that we reached this compression after such an expensive path is a failure of installation, not a lack of prior intelligence. OMNI repeatedly found pieces of all four. It never gave them one owned address and an enforcement chain.

## Assistant

**Yes — pressure it before we deploy it, not during. And it should replace something rather than be added on.**

Knox put the blind counter-design inside G1. That's the wrong moment. The highest-value time to have three fresh instances design this from scratch is **before we commit to the plan**, not after the integrator is appointed and four gates are already running. If three independent designs converge on a shape our arc can't produce, that's a defect in the arc and it costs three prompts to find out. So it moved to G-PRE, ahead of G0 acceptance.

It also collapses your question and Knox's item into one exercise. You asked "should a fresh agent look at the plan." Knox asked for a blind design of the problem. **The blind design subsumes the plan review** — anything three independent designs produce that our arc can't reach *is* a plan defect. Doing both would be two blind exercises stacked, which is the ceremony we keep swearing off.

One honest limit I put in writing rather than discovering later: a blind instance handed a facts-only brief produces **generic** frontier architecture. It's strong at finding what we omitted and nearly useless at judging what we got right that generic practice gets wrong. So the exercise is scoped to the strong half, and Knox's inverse question is doing the real work — *which parts of your proposal break because healthcare has legally independent principals whose truths and refusals can't be collapsed into one platform.* Without that, a frontier model hands us one ontology, one workflow engine, one control plane, one event graph. The god-layer, wearing better clothes.

**On the four laws — they're written down. Now. In the plan, verbatim, as of this commit.**

Knox proposed preserving them as a "required G2 deliverable." That's still evaporation, and you'd have been right to be furious about it — G2 is several gates away, inside a plan, inside a PR nobody has accepted. That's exactly the shape of the last six months. So the text is in §0.5 now; **G2 relocates it to `/architecture/README.md`, it doesn't author it.** Explicit, Resolvable, Evolvable, Observable — and each one is wired to a specific acceptance test so none of them is decoration.

And your bigger point stands, so let me say the honest version of it: **we never lacked those four.** Explicit is already `GRD-033`/`GRD-034`. Resolvable is the exact question the effective-architecture compiler exists to answer. Evolvable is Build OS Step-5, accepted months ago. Observable is drift detection. All four existed as fragments in four different places and **not once as a single statement with an owner.** That's not a failure of intelligence across six months — it's the same installation failure as everything else in this arc, aimed at the arc's own conclusion. Which is either the most damning thing in this thread or the most encouraging one, depending on whether the fix holds.

Byte normalization is done — the three stale references Knox found are gone, the sweep is clean, and the charter now carries **zero** gate bodies. One sequence, one place: G-PRE → G0 → G1 → G2 → G3 → G4.

My honest read on cost, since you raised it: G-PRE is cheap and should happen. G1 through G3 are the expensive part, and roughly half of that is *classification*, which parallelizes well across agents because it's mechanical. The part that genuinely can't be rushed is G1's convergence and G3's foundational reconciliation — and if G-PRE comes back `PLAN_MATERIALLY_INCOMPLETE`, better to eat that now than at G3.

Insurance still frozen. `C3.9` and `E2` untouched. No integrator appointment requested — that's still waiting on the review, correctly.

Ruling

Yes—run fresh pre-pressure before G0.

But Opus’s current formulation is still wrong in one important way:

A blind counter-design does not subsume a review of the plan.

Those are different tests.

* A blind design reveals architecture we may not have imagined.
* An unblinded plan audit reveals whether this particular plan is overbuilt, internally contradictory, poorly sequenced, dependent on unavailable authority, or incapable of producing what it promises.

We need both, but we do not need another army of agents or another recursive review cycle.

The right preflight uses two fresh agents

Use two fresh instances from different model families. Each performs two stages:

You were right that we conjoined two things, and Knox was right to reject it. Withdrawn. A blind design and a plan audit answer different questions — one finds what we never imagined and can't tell you whether the plan runs; the other finds ceremony and bad sequencing and can't find what we failed to conceive. Both run now, two agents, two stages each: Stage A blind and frozen, Stage B unblinded with the real packet plus their own frozen answer.

**Your comparator point is the one that changed the structure.** A comparator built and then discarded before the artifact gets written is the Insurance failure, exactly. So every finding from both blind submissions becomes a row in a reconciliation ledger, and **G1 and G3 cannot close while any row is undisposed** — adopted, adopted-narrowed, already-present with the carrier named, rejected with reason, out-of-scope with a destination, or open with an owner. That's not new machinery; it's Gate-1b's own "named consuming gate" rule pointed at the preflight. PRE-0 feeds the authoring gates, not just G0.

**On your three-step process — there are five inputs, and the two you didn't name are the cheap ones.** Consider what it should be, inventory what it's trying to be, comparator pressure — those are yours and they're right. The two missing: **the failure record** and **the consumer requirements**. First principles gives you what's elegant. Comparators give you what's conventional. Neither gives you what survives *our* specific failure modes, and we have nine named ones and six months of receipts sitting right there for free. And designing from the cold entrant rather than the author is the only reason routing is testable at all — architecture written for its author is precisely why the estate is unnavigable.

**The files exist. Not promised — created.**

- The protocol file carries the **exact Stage-A brief to paste verbatim** and the **seven Stage-B questions**.
- Two empty drop files with provenance tables that force declaring whether Stage A was frozen before Stage B ran, and whether the agent saw the plan or the other agent's work. If Stage A wasn't frozen first, Stage B is invalid and the table says so.
- The reconciliation ledger, with a **separate table for the inverse question** — where each generic design breaks under legally independent principals. That's the half that finds what frontier practice gets wrong about healthcare rather than what we got wrong.

Two things I'd flag about the preflight before you run it. The Stage-B prompt demands **both** fatal omissions **and** removable machinery, because an audit that can only add scope isn't an audit — that's how this plan would quietly double in size. And the honest limit stays on the record: a blind instance given a facts-only brief produces *generic* frontier architecture. It's strong at finding what we omitted and close to useless at judging what we got right that generic practice would get wrong. Which is why the inverse question isn't a nicety — it's where half the value is.

Knox's defect rule replaced mine and his is better: the plan is defective only where it **cannot express, evaluate, adopt, reject or disposition** a materially necessary capability the counter-design surfaces. Difference is evidence, not authority. Otherwise two blind agents hand us one ontology and one control plane and we'd be obligated to take it seriously.

Hard stop is written in: one reconciliation, at most one bounded amendment, then G0. No recursive blind rerun unless an amendment changes the fundamental decomposition. After that, stop designing the design process.

Nine files on PR #15. Insurance frozen, `C3.9` and `E2` untouched, no integrator appointment — that still waits for the review, which at this point is the only thing left blocking G0.

## Assistant

All three fixed and pushed.

**On the save problem — nothing is read-only.** The files are `rw-r--r--`, owned by ubuntu, no git hooks, no `.gitattributes`. The cause is almost certainly that **they only exist on the FAI branch.** If your local checkout is on `main`, those files aren't in your working tree at all, so there's nothing to save into:

```bash
git fetch origin && git checkout cursor/fai-foundational-architecture-30f4
```

Ten files appear under `.cursor/plans/`. If you're editing through GitHub's web view instead, that requires a commit per save, which is its own misery — pull the branch locally.

**You were right about the carriers and it's a bad miss.** Opening `agent_a_verbatim.md` cold told you nothing: no prompt, no source, no idea who sent traffic there. The prompt lived in a different file and the carrier didn't even link to it. That is blind incoming traffic — the exact unrouted-artifact failure this whole arc exists to kill, committed inside the arc's own files. Each carrier now embeds the **exact prompt verbatim in §2**, names the protocol as source of record, names the reconciliation ledger as its consumer, and records who ran it and whether the prompt was modified.

**And you were right that the blindness questions were useless.** Six fields and not one asked whether the agent was blind to the **repository** or blind to the **internet**. An agent with repo access can read our decomposition — it isn't blind. An agent that searched the web for "OMNI architecture" isn't blind either. Neither voids a submission, but if we don't know, then "convergence" from an agent that read our answer looks identical to real convergence. Now declared per carrier: fresh context · blind to repo · blind to internet · blind to the OMNI name · blind to plan/charter/Reactor/root-requirements · blind to the failure record · blind to the other agents · clarifying questions asked · tool calls made. Agent C's version inverts those correctly and adds repo access, ref inspected, and whether load-bearing claims were actually verified.

**The two retired thread files needed a different fix, not the same one.** They're conversations, not runs — there's no prompt to embed and no blindness to declare, because both seats were anchored the entire time, which is the whole reason PRE-0 exists. So their provenance now asks what actually applies: model, session dates, date pasted, **complete or excerpted — and if excerpted, what was cut**, and whether anything was redacted. That last pair matters, because a partial paste that claims to be verbatim is worse than no paste.

Everything's on PR #15, head `06f1e6f`. Pull the branch and the paste should just work.
